speaker: Rob Moore
words: Well, what were the different jobs that the men did on a thrashing crew?

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: Well, when I first started out, my brother, they used to come down off of the ridge. Well, Martin Thomas had a thrashing machine, a horsepower machine. And from this horsepower equipment, a tumbling rod went to the thrashing machine and run the machine. And my brother, at those days he was young, but he was always around the machine and working. And a few years later, he got jobs going out and help oil on the thrashing machine.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: What did the oiler do?

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: He'd oil the whole machine. See if any of the bearings got hot. And at noon, when it stood still, oil all the bearings. And just keep it in shape. But he was also really interested in just the running of it and seemed to catch on off easy about it. And so this fellow that really the machine operator run it, he'd feed it out of that on his oiler. And so help him out too. And so he started that way. And then later on, I come in too and I went out and pitched bundles. Those days we got $2.25 an hour and started a day. A day, yes, that's right. And get up early in the morning and dip the water out of a barrel and wash and have breakfast and either start it out six o'clock or maybe even before. And then about in the mid-forenoon, they'd come out with a lunch, about five minutes to ten minutes to stop. And then at noon, an hour, afternoon, had another lunch. And then thrashed it, kind of get dark, then go in and have feed and go to bed. Except I remember one time that I was out in the Hall of Muddle and the straw stack caught a fire. And they moved the machine over on the, kind of on the sloping slope. They moved it over on the other side of the valley and set up and didn't take them long. It was going again. They had the fire, let the fire burn down on the straw stack. They had to surround it. Well, I lighted it up the machine, so I think we thrashed till nine or ten o'clock that night because it had light.

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: Then later on, I'd usually go out, help on the separator or something like that. And while I went out and pitched bundles, and sometimes I had a team out and hall bundles, and at the time I bucked straw, and I was hauling the straw to the engine because it burned straw. And then also when I catch up with the straw, I usually help the fireman relieve him. Because we had to punch straw in there with the fork, just keep pushing it in as fast as it burned. And if the steam went down, you just pushed it in a little faster. And if the steam got up and you slowed down a little, that's about the way it went.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: Did they start the fire with straw too? Did they start with wood or coal or something to get it going? What? Did they start the fire with straw too?

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: Yeah, they just started the fire out, not the straw gloves. Later, some of them burned coal off, but mostly all burned straw in those days. But they burned coal or wood when they were moving in one place or the other. And they'd usually burn coal or wood.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: Well, the straw buck would help the fireman out when the fireman got any... The straw buck would help the fireman out when the wood was getting caught up?

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: Yeah, the straw buck, it generally wasn't really his job, but he generally would do that because the fireman was pretty steady there just to keep that going. And the straw buck, if it wasn't pulling too heavy or it had good burning straw or something, why he didn't need as much straw and he had a little time in between. And they'd usually sometimes help the fireman out and let the fireman go get him a drink or one thing or another. And even for the fun of it, it just seemed like about what fire liked to do. The first machines I remember, the horse power machine, they had... They didn't blow the straw out like they do now. There was a draper... This is a combine you're talking about. Oh, the threshing machine. The horses went round and round. And this machine had a draper which carried the straw out the ways and then they had one or two men on a straw pile to make a straw stack. And also to feed these bundles, they laid there and there was... I think there was one man on each side with his knife and they cut the bands on the bundles. And stuck them in head first and spread them out and stuck them in carefully so they went too even. So it was kind of a smaller set up those days. And then they come out later with knives that cut the bands and they just threw them down in there. And then later they come out with a blower on it and blew the straw out after they got to using steam engines on them. And most of them got to be steam engines. And then later some of them went to gasoline. I believe some of them burned diesel. I'm not too sure. But I think it is... They didn't call it diesel, they called it distillate. It just went a little different I guess with that burn.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: Well after the grain went through the thrashing machine, what happened to it then?

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: Well the grain, there was a spout that came down first and it hooked a sack on it. It switched. There's two spouts and they could switch from one side of the sack holder to another. And there would be a sack put on the spout and that would be filling while they put a new sack on the other spout. And the total last, they had the bigger machines and the thrash faster. They also had what they called a two sack sores and a jig. The sack sores would usually sew up two sacks and put them down and go back a little ways and that's what they'd sit on. And then the jig would put a sack, to start out with, he'd put a sack on each one of the fillers and he'd let one of them fill. And just as soon as that one got full enough, he'd jig it down and carry it over to one of the sack sores.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: What was jigging it down?

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: Just to settle it down and get it about the right full. And so if he spilled any, if he had too much in there, he'd scoop it out on the ground under him so it wouldn't clean up. But it'd be there where he was. And then he'd carry that sack, just lift it to the top and carry it five or ten feet to wherever the sack sores were. And they'd sit there and he'd set it between their knees and they'd kind of get their knees around it and then they'd sew it up. And then they'd bounce it up on their knees and then get up and put it over on the sack pile. Carried it off maybe ten or fifteen, twenty feet to wherever they started the sack pile. And when this jig, when one sack had get full, he'd have an empty sack on the other place where it'd come out. He'd switch so it'd put the grain into that sack while he'd jig this one down and carry it over to the sack sores and then put another new sack on it. But that time the other sack was about full and he'd jig that down, carry it over to the other sack sores and put empty sacks on it and that's the one back and forth.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: So he never got much of a pause then either? He never got much of a rest then either?

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: No, they never got any rest unless something broke down or something that sometimes something like that would help out a little bit.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: Well, was the oiler always busy too? Was he kept busy just oily?

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: You see Mike, the oiler and the separator tender, they were just mostly always watching and see if something needed and then sometimes they'd have a bearing at that start to heat or something. He'd oil that ever occasionally oftener and just kind of look over the thing and usually in the noon hour then they'd go through it and oil it completely again. And if there's anything needed adjusting or something like that, they'd adjust it up again and try to get going in the afternoon again until lunch time and then they'd have lunch in the forenoon. First they used to, at our place, and we had the cashews there, they were not as small, the mother always had a cook for them and they boarded them. They usually went home in the evening, but there was quite a crew. In those days, I was really first in thinking about it. A hot stove there in the kitchen, you know, and then in the dining room, all the tables around and people were eating there. You can imagine how warm it would be there. It was really warm and they had an hour noon and they'd try to eat as fast as they could and get out and cool off enough and then get out and go to work again. But later they got the cook houses up on the ridges and there was always two cooks and they'd have the lunch and the meals there at the cook house. They had what they called a flunky, he was a roust about, and he'd get the food and get whatever they needed and water and things like that. Then they also had a water book that had a tank and he'd haul water for the engine and keep it to go in. It took quite a few people to run an out shift after they had one precise quick lift until the combines come.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: How long would it take them to build up steam again in the morning before they can get started?

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: Oh, it's kind of hard, I guess, and I don't know. I never started running a station machine, but we run a tramway and had something similar to it. We could get up steam in 20-25 minutes with kindling and wood and fuel, but I wouldn't exactly know if this was taking the station machine. I'd say half an hour 45 minutes, but that would be more or less of a guess.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: Would the firemen get out earlier than everybody else then and get working?

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: Yeah, yeah. Some of them then had a watchman at night and I think he started the fire. Now, I might be wrong on that, but I kind of believe it did, to have somebody that looked around and done different things that had to be done through the night so they could get started in the morning.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: Was he watching for fires or what?

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: I don't know whether they, I'm not sure, but whether they used some wood or coal to put in there to hold a fire overnight or whether they started anew in the morning. But it seemed like they were always ready to go when we were pitching bundles. We never got a chance to see if they were ready to go.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: About how long, until when were the thrashing machines coming down here? Until about what year were you working with thrashing machines?

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: Well, I remember I got a picture where on our home place, Martin Thomas came down and this picture was taken, I believe it was in 1895. And that was a horsepower rig. It used to be on American Ridge. I believe that there was only one on the end of the ridge. I used to come down there. And then about 1910, I believe it was, I think Ottawa started to grow up about 1907 or 1908 as oiling. And about 1910 or 1911, I would either go out and pitch bundles or go out in the hall bundles or buck straw for a number of years. And then when that wound up, maybe even before, toward later years, we would run the tramway. And just as soon as they started the hall towards the warehouse, we would go and take care of the warehouse and run the tramway. And that, we kind of quit the thrashing there and then went to the trimming business. All of that. We handled it after they had it in the sacks.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: Were there ever any serious accidents with that tramway? Did it ever get away?

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: No, it got away before my times. Mother said that it got away some way. At the upper end of it, it went up the hill and then it came in a little more on a, not so steep, more on a flat. And it seemed as though when they stopped it, the car, some way, I've heard different stories. I've heard that they had the lower one unhooked and they couldn't hold it. And I've heard that they backed it up some way and that car put slack in the cable and unhooked and took off. But Mother said that she was hanging out clothes and she heard a noise and all she could see on the side hill over there was a bunch of dust. And it seemed like this car went on down and there was a...

speaker: Rob Moore
words: It was an empty car or a full car?

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: This is full. And it was steep and at the bottom of the steep pitch there was a bench out that went out a little ways. And it seemed as though when it hit that bench it told me that it took right straight out and left the track and went out in space. And just scattered everything it was down and over the hillside there. And that part now, whether... My idea is more or less that it just got away from them, that I don't know why they unhooked it or just they didn't have any safety hooks on it or something. It got away in a way. Or else if it was that they didn't fasten the lower one, why then of course just the cable itself came up and there was a car on it. So they told me when they first started out they used block and tackle and I believe a horse and pulled the top car out off of this level of place until it got to the front of the hill and then the loaded car would bring an empty one up. But that didn't prove out very good and then they put in this steam engine. They had a twin silver engine with two drums and the cable would come up and keep going back and forth. They'd go back under and go around the back drum and then go around the front one, back the back one, around the front one, back forth about a dozen times or so until it went back out again. And then they had band brakes on it and the engine could be turned on or off and whenever the load got out to the front of the hill they could uncouple the engine and just hold it with the brake that it coasts down. And they'd get dumped to track once in a while but otherwise, in my time, there was at one time before some way a car came down and bumped something out and some timbers fell on somebody and heard him I remember one time. But otherwise, as cars were fixed, you couldn't hardly get off of the cable. If it did get out into the brush at the top, what we usually have to do is fire up and get up a little more steam but they had engine enough there to pull a full car right out of the brush back up again. And they'd put it up a ways and work it back onto the rails and sometimes it had to even have to unload it to get it on and then put it on there.

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: It was quite a triumph there after the trucks came in. It broke loose when it did get us started. The rails just started to keep on coming and just doubled around on the side hill over there. And one fella that was up on the side hill helping to long get us started, he said he'd take behind the tree and he said the rails would just come on both sides there. They'd double up around the tree and everything else. Brothers got a picture of it right at the time being there's a rail sticking in a tree up there. The end of the rail went into that tree. I don't know how far but the coupling had taken apart where the coupling was and there's about two or three feet sticking out of that tree now in that tree where that went in there. And we used to like to run that tramways. It was quite a job nowadays. They work entirely different. We lived just across from that warehouse. It takes us about ten minutes on the bicycle to get over to the lower warehouse and then walk up the tram and get steam up by seven o'clock. We usually leave the house at six o'clock and get over to the warehouse about ten minutes after six and walk up that hill over the hillside to the top in about twenty minutes to be up there at half past. Start a fire in the boiler and load the first car out. And then whatever help you had either one or two men they'd come up on the first tram then but the first tram always run just like at seven o'clock. And then at night the help rode down on the last tram and then the fella had to walk down to get down those days so I didn't have automobiles or if we didn't have last year we'd run and we had motorcycles before but he didn't even dawn on us to ride a motorcycle around. We just took up the track and made our money. We got thirty cents an hour, three dollars a day. That was good money those days. Got up there and but on going down there was days that didn't run the tram but just went up to the upper warehouse to receive green when the farmers brought it in. And so I got on on me that I could make a rigging ride down and I took some two befores, four befores and tore them off of the warehouse up for different places and put them on the rail lengthwise about three, four, four feet long and nailed one before or something on the inside for a flange. Nailed a board across the back for a seat and nailed two two by sixes across from the front with the space in between them and so that then made a sled that fit on the track and they couldn't jump off. And then we take it out to the front of the hill and a bit of piece of rod like this letter S and then hook it between the space between the two front timbers and put a pipe hook it around the cable underneath. There's always a cable laid between one track or the other and then use a pipe on top and lift at this table cable up underneath and then use that for a break and so that worked fine. And so every time that there's any slack, we had one of those jiggers up there but every time we had to go up and receive green we'd make another one. And by the time we got through we had five or six of them and then whenever the first tram run it was loaded all back and hauled them back up again. And there's quite an incident happened there one time that this is E.W. Porter owned this warehouse, also the banker, and there was a circus coming to town in the afternoon and school was out I guess that day. And Porter told us it seemed like all the farmers was coming down to the circus that we didn't have to tram that afternoon if we're tramming the forenoon. Why if we could if it was all right with the farmers up there and that they wasn't going to haul or talk it over with them why go to circus. So this boy Marion Porter, he was a young fella, he wanted to ride down with me. He says I'd like to ride down with you when we go down on one of those we call them go devils. And so he stayed up there when we were running the last tram and we took it out the front of the hill and we got on it. And the first place is steep, starts out steep and there's this bench down below. And as we started down this steep place, tried to slow it down and this rod, as we had been a little bit, it started to straighten out. And so I told him I says now don't make any difference how fast we go and when we hit that bench we're going to have to get off. But I'll slow it down the best I can. And so I told him when I said go, I said you get off on your side, you get ready and I'll get off over here. And so I got down there and I got to slow down pretty well but they're still going and I was smitten about, you know, get off and he got off on one side and I got off on the other. And we bumped a little bit to ourselves but not heard anything.

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: But I can still hear him when it went down through there in the desperate fly and he says gee, he says aren't you glad we ain't on it now? And it went right down there and went in and knocked onto the bumper and knocked the bumper right into the lower car. And just hit the end of it and it smashed itself, all the pieces down there. We had to walk down and hustle away. After that whenever we rode double well we took two of them and tied them together and instead of using a hook we put a wire around it. We'd wrap a bunch of wire but that is always singing. You could hear it all over the valley when you come down and you can hear that thing that's singing the way that the wire is going down sliding over the cable. And we had a lot of fun out of it too.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: Well, there were a series of pretty bad train wrecks around here too weren't there? Wasn't there a series of pretty bad train wrecks around here? Wasn't there a series of pretty bad train wrecks around here?

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: Oh, train wrecks… yes, there was a train wreck at the, when they were building, I believe it was a line that runs up to Clearwater to States. I believe that is the one. They hung rails down for it and there was up a Troy and I've heard different stories. They said that they didn't want to take a chance of going down. It was frosty and one thing and another. But anyway, there was order to go down with the rails and they came down and they couldn't hold it. And as he got down towards up front and towards Kendrick up here, the conductor, he had cut the caboose loose and held him around and saved himself and it another fellow. And the rest of it kept on going and they went, they do rail right up above in the upper end of Kendrick here and went into the Potlatch Creek. And I think there was two or three of them engineers, both of the engineering firemen I believe it was. And I've got more accurate data of it someplace. That was killed and then they had one or two hearings, trials. This fellow cut himself loose with the caboose and it seemed as though he got canned because he figured if he'd have kept that caboose on, how to hold the tail end back with it. It had been all right too, but it was quite a mess. I can just remember of going up and see the engines laying in there. And it had just been a few years ago. They just stood a rail. They were working in that quick and there was still a rail down in there. It was down in there. I've got a picture of that. I've also got the story of this wreck and also of the trial.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: Well, Kendrick had quite a few problems in the early days with fires and floods and stuff like that too, didn't it? Didn't Kendrick have quite a problem in the early days with fire and floods and stuff like that?

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: Well, it seemed like he didn't have as much trouble with fires as he had later on because he didn't have any equipment to set anything apart much. Smoking was the only thing. And it seemed like those days that more smoke of pipe or something, or cigar and smoke was not a twerk time. But there wasn't as much out. They did catch it. It seemed like the only trouble they had would be a straw stack catch of fires or something like that. But later on now with these trucks and one thing and another, the exhaust, I think that's where they catch it, threw out some sparkers. This set will accumulate and then a hot one will go out into the dry grass and set to the fire. The hardest job of mine was pulling a machine a lot of times from one place to another. The kind of ditches and uphill and one thing and another, they'd hook it up and pull it with the engine. But as if they had a cost, I remember the cost down there to brought in a new machine one time with Juliaetta. And they were going to throw a shower home place down there first. That was about 1912 or so, I'd say, 11 or 12. And unloaded it down there to Juliaetta. Then they couldn't go across the bridges with it. They had to kind of make a road on side and hold the front of the engine down so it didn't rear up, going up out of the bank and it's quite a chore there. It caused ditches like that to get them from one place to the other. It was all right in the fields when they could go from one field to the other. But I had to go further. It was kind of hard to get anyone down to where we were some years. We always tried to find out ahead of time whether we were going to be able to get anyone to thrash because then we'd just have to take the hay. So down in the place there, it's hard to get out. But it used to be that you'd be here in about noon. You'd hear the whistles blow, three or four of them around. You'd slice the machines over.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: There were quite a few floods here in the early days, weren't there?

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: Yes… it used to be that we'd earn a few dollars once in a while. We'd got bigger when they'd have some floods or wash outs. And especially on one in 1911, I remember down there that had a cloud burst. It covered up the tracks. They run the trains in on each side, the passenger trains, and transferred and carried everything from one side to the other. They used to get a job helping doing that. Then they had it shoveled out so the trains could get through. It seemed like hot water had come up. Then they had the gulch and it would cover the tracks up every so often. We'd be called out to help shovel them out. So we got pretty good pay. We always liked to sit in mind when they did get covered up. That place for a while there seemed to bother, but in earlier years, I can remember about 1900 or 1901, there was two wash outs there. One of the years, a work train came down with a cook house and some sleeping cars. They just had a caboose and some car or two with the tools and hand cars. They were going down below Juliaetta, but as they got this side of Juliaetta, there on Middle Potlatch Creek, a bridge had washed out. They couldn't go any further, so they were going to go back to Kendrick. But by that time, they had washed the track out just about a quarter of a mile behind them. They couldn't get it back. So in the evening, there was a lady cook and her husband, they came up to our place. There were some others that needed sleep for the night. They came up and they slept in a barn. And the others stayed down and watched to see what was going, and they'd run what they had left. First, they took the caboose and took the cars in one after the other during the night. They'd run that engine ahead and just keep it, and they saved it. I think one car or two, the rest of it went in. But as this went in, there was just above where the bridge was. They took the bridge out. And then, of course, that bridge went into the river and the cars. And it went down and took the railroad bridge out, little further. It went to the tramway, and that gave them still more. And it went down and took the bridge out at Juliaetta by the depot. And on this setup, there was the caboose, and a couple of cars were over Caustic Creek, about where the tramway was, just a little below where it went in. And one or two went in and landed down below Juliaetta, hung up on a place down there. And then later, they came down with the equipment and pulled them over and put them back on the tracks again and got it out. Now, we used to go over there and play in that caboose. It was sitting there in kind of a sand pile, leaning towards one side. And it went in and kind of made you feel dizzy and kind of goofy. But it always makes me think of going, and we should have bought that caboose because I went in places and they showed me where water would run uphill and the ball would roll uphill. But that's what it did in that caboose. We used to go in there. And because it sure made you think of the stuff, the optical illusion there, it made you think that the stuff rolled uphill. So we should have bought that caboose and then put up a sign and had something. But I don't know why they took it out. And I still remember the name of the people that – Neff was the name of the cook and his wife. They seemed to be nice people. Some way I just remembered their name. And then I believe it was the next year, I'd say either the year before or the year afterwards. One was in 1900, I think, one in 1901. ... that located at U.S. came to U.S. at the locate. And they had two – they came on a train, but when they got to Troy, the tracks had washed out to Kendrick and they couldn't get any further. And it was muddy in the wintertime – springtime, I think it was. And so they hired livery rigs, two livery rigs, two hacks to bring their trunks and stuff, and I think there's eight in their family at the time. And they brought them down in the muddy roads and they couldn't get to Juliaetta because the bridge had washed out on middle pod lights there.

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: So where's the first place located on the other side? It looked like they were able to put up a few of them so they'd stop, come back that far. And the folks made room for them some way and loaded their stuff there and the livery rigs went on back. And they stayed a couple, three days till some were fixed so they could get across the creek down there. But they made it out all right. Some of them slept in the barn. But they often mentioned about it, how far they knew, how they got there and stayed there and remembered the place. And so that's the two. And then they had other washouts. Later years I've got some pictures of washout below Juliaetta down about four miles where I took out, and I tracked it all the way laying in the creek for about a couple hundred yards and down below Juliaetta where the water's over the rails. And up here at the depot where the water was, you couldn't see any ties, just the top of the rails stuck out. But it always would do damage someplace along that there wouldn't be any trains for a couple, three days. And in 1927, I had a wet snow up in the Bovill Country, I believe it was Thanksgiving Day. And then it rained into it and the wind came into it and it all came down through here and it washed the track out just below the Juliaetta Depot. And a work train went down and engine rolled in and one or two cars, I think, with it. And also a year or two later, the first of April I had a flood that went over the tracks, washed out different places. And Kendrick was isolated, couldn't get either direction. They brought the mail up with a plane and dropped it up on a hillside here. So as far as washouts and train wrecks and something, it's kind of an interesting place. And then of course there was a train wreck that they had when they were building a state's railroad, I believe it was the state's branch over there that was coming down with a number, quite a few cars of rails and iron and they had two engines on it. And when they left Troy, they didn't think they'd make it, but they told him to go on. But as they got down there, they couldn't hold it. And the caboose fella, the conductor, he kept the caboose loose and he got it stopped. But the rest of the train came down and just today as the town appeared, both engines rolled in. And I don't know how many people it killed. I think it was both engineers and both firemen. And I can remember seeing and laying in there, I have a picture of it too, where they're taking it out afterwards. And also that they had a trial on this fella that cut his caboose loose. He wasn't supposed to do that. If he'd have left it on, they figured it might have had back enough to go on. And as far as I believe the history is that they fired him. And that was one of the biggest. I can remember one morning that they called up an R.H. Porter down here at Juliaetta and told him that the engine got away from him up a Troy, was heading down the tracks. And if it got that far, they wanted him to go over there right away and put some ties on the track. There's a stack of ties down there, across from where he lived, to put him on there some way so they could wreck that train or that engine so it couldn't go any further. And he did that, but it didn't get that far. It stopped up above here, and I was told that it seemed like they bumped it on a sidetrack up there. And it lost some of the wheels under the coal car or something. And it didn't let drugs and that had a ... enough so that it didn't get this far. Another time, I can remember that it was coming between here and Juliaetta. And a bunch of cars went by, maybe there were four cars loaded with cattle. It went by a pretty good link of speed, faster than the train usually goes. And pretty soon, the engine came along while afterwards behind it, but it seemed like they went pretty careful. It wasn't going too fast. But in about a couple of hours, this engine came back, bringing those cars and cattle back up again. They'd got down below Arrow, where it got leveller, and it ran back into the freight train. And the freight train was also traveling, so it was lucky and went out. And we got a lot of kids, things to see like that those days, the wrecks. Here not too many years ago, they had, I believe it was a snowplow, but they had tied on the back, a couple of them were out or something, and they tied it on the back of a freight train that went up to Kendrick. And it got up above about a mile, a little over a mile, while I had broke loose and went on down the track. So they backed the train up, the freight train up. In order to get it, to catch it, they backed it up and away, but the freight train then jumped the track on the corner. And two or three cars or frozen food went down over the bank about a hundred feet. Of course, they immediately got some refrigerated automobiles, trucks, and got the stuff out, and then later put the cars back up on the tracks.

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: And then there's usually fires along the tracks up there used to be that the engines had sparked, brakes had sparked, and they had trouble. The railroad had quite a time of troubles, you might say, between Arrow and just above Kendrick here, that down at, I've got some pictures of where there's a track down here about four miles below Juliaetta. It must be, oh, a couple, 300 yards where the track is laying in the river, and underwashed it, and it just settled down in. And down below Juliaetta where the water was over the railroad and over the highway, and it's been quite often that we'd have no train service on kind of high water. And in town here at, at 19, one or two, 19 one, I believe it was, that it washed across up here where that train went in. Some way I've heard that they damaged the fill or something, they called it quickback, and the way the quick come through up there and came down through town. And I know left about a foot or two of mud in the store, I just remember being up here one time with mother at McCrew's store. It stood where the park now is, there was mud in there, mud had to get out of the store. And down here, right at the first turn, the street down here, there was Hamlin or Hamley, lived there. And Fred Crocker went in to rescue them. Out, they were surrounded with water with a team buggy. And as he came out, the buggy, I guess, something came down and hit the buggy and also went into a hole underneath. And two of the children spilled out and they drowned.

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: So it wasn't always this washing. Now this, I don't know if I mentioned this train about at Arrow, there's high water, and it washed out quite a stretch of track there and put it over on the other side of the creek. The whole thing bridging all of the bridges of Howard Gulch. It just undermined it all and it just swung over on the other side of the river, there's on a turn. And they built a new track, filled in to build a new track in there. And so it wasn't really, we had some more, a little high water afterwards, but it wasn't really what to consider high water. But anyway, it had underwashed some of this fill that they made right at that place. And as the passenger train went down at night, about 10, 30, 11 o'clock, they even had a baggage car and a mail car and two or three passenger cars. I have a picture of that too there. But they went in, the engine rolled in, and the first cars, they didn't uncouple but at this, the last ones was on the track and I saw them halfway down, the engine was down. And they never did find a fireman, his name was Skidmore, I remember. And I don't remember where the engineer got out or whether he was grounded, but it was a bad wreck. It didn't materialize. Well, in those railroad days, it was interesting to think about the transportation when there'd be maybe a hundred Italians on the crew. They'd have these hand cars, pump cars, and they'd have maybe a couple dozen of them together, tied together, and they'd go up and down the tracks on them, singing and having a good time of pumping away. Instead of running them single, they all had them tied together and all, everybody was pumping those things, going up and down the tracks, going. And all this railroad work was done by pump cars like that. And take them up town here, they couldn't pump them up. So they'd have a flat car, and when the morning passenger came up, sometime between eight and nine o'clock, they had a rope and they'd put this rope around something on the back of the passenger train. And we got to the furthest end of their job, and they'd cut themselves loose and do their work. And then all they needed to do was get on and hold a break, coming down, and they could come back home again in the evenings. But a little later on, they made them stop doing that, and they'd come out then with the gasoline rakes.

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: And it went that way. It used to be to take a train about an hour to go from Kendrick to Troy, 11, 12 miles. I remember that we were on a picnic, oh, this was about 1915, 1916, up above Kendrick about a couple of three miles. And the passenger train came up and had one or two cars of fruit, refrigerator fruit on it. And it was coming at a slow speed. And another boy and I went down and we'd come on these fruit cars, and we rode up the track quite a ways. We saw a push car down there on the side, sitting inside the track. We got up, walked, got up a little further up, but we walked down this push car, and it had a hole knocked out that you could take a pole or something and put a brake onto one of the wheels with it. So we got it on the track, and we rode back down to where the picnic was on that push car. And we used to play around on the railroad track quite a lot. And with every slow we used to on our work, telephone work, we'd go up a applied spur about three miles above town, and we'd just get off most of a lot of the places. We knew about where the train would slow down quite a lot, and we'd always get off.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: Were there, as a kid, you say you used to ride the train around a lot as a kid? You say you used to ride the train quite a bit as a kid?

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: Yeah, and we rode the train. The train was full. It'd be fourth of July celebration, and the best place between ... and Kendrick, just didn't have standing room hardly. And it'd be clear for ten cents, one way, fifteen cents for a round trip. I've got some tickets dated 1912 yet that some way they didn't use or they didn't take up. And yeah, it used to be by train, they'd go into work, go train, they'd go to the worst of New Spokane or someplace to go by train. And we used to come up here and roller skate, I can remember in early years. And two of us, three of us, or four, we'd come up here, and we'd always buy a return trip ticket. We'd get them cheaper, and they were good for a month, and we always had one or two in our pocket either way. But anyway, we'd go out on the back platform in the winter, and they wouldn't come out to take tickets there because they didn't know there was a ticket as anyone out there, so we'd say you had that ticket again for the next time. Well, one time I remember that there was a couple more fellows came with us, and we all went out on the back platform. They went along too, and the conductor came out, and these fellows thought they were going to get the ride for nothing, you know. Well, the conductor got, we had tickets the rest of us because we always had one, but it's one fellow, I remember, he didn't have a ticket, so the conductor took his hat, and he told him the next morning he'd come down there and bring his dime, and he'd give him his hat back. So we rushed to Ten Cents and paid his way, I think there was two of them. Well, that, as young as you know, they'll always figure out something, so we'll have a little fun. There was about eight or ten of us got on that train, and we passed the conductor, and all but two of them got out the back and jumped off and walked down to Juliaetta. And they just wanted to see what happened, and he said the two, and Brother was one of them, another one they wanted to see, said that they hunted all the way to Juliaetta under the seats in every place, and looking for the rest of those guys. We were just on our way a foot, going down to Juliaetta. We thought that was a pretty good joke.

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: As we used to, I remember on telephone work, we used to go on passenger train down to Arrow and then catch a passenger train up to Myrtle on the other side, and then walk across the hill over there. You could go up and ride on on this other side and have a team meet you on the other side of the quick, about four mile below Juliaetta and come back again. Other times, we'd have trouble down towards Arrow. We'd go down there and play horseshoe down there. Somebody had a horseshoe set down there until a freight train came up, and we'd get on that freight train. But sometime, they wouldn't stop here. It usually stopped to take water we could get off. But we lived at Juliaetta. We had to walk from here to Juliaetta back, but that beat walking all the way. But I remember one time where they didn't stop, but as soon as they got on the hill up here, they slowed down enough so we could get off. We had a little further to walk, but still wasn't as far as walking home from Arrow. We used to ride that freight train back every once in a while and get on it. Sometimes they'd never see us, and if they did tell them what they did, they'd usually just call it a good evening at a section boss. He'd notice a speeder to use on a track. He had a little hand speeder, had rubber tires on it to go back and forth. They'd hold out more. They wouldn't dare to do anything like that. If something had happened, they'd sue them for the rest of what they were worth, you know, and anything else. But those days, everybody helped together more. There wasn't anyone like that to take his own chances, and that's the way it was. When we'd go up on the passenger train and tell the conductor, we're just going to jump off up there. He said, Be careful. He'd usually come out when we jumped off. The section crew used to go up on the train in the wintertime and jump off into the snow or someplace, so they'd step off and jump off.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: When you were riding the freights, did you ever run across any freight bums or hobos or anything like that?

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: Oh, yes. They'd be hobos here most all the time. They'd come in here and get something at the back door or something on the tracks. But I always figured a hobo, the reason he was a hobo is because he wasn't a crook. He was making an honest living. He wasn't because this guy is a steal, but a hobo wasn't steal much and always makes me think of Pearly Cheney, if Troy came up there one day. I worked pretty slick on a guy this morning. He was always dressed up in old clothes. He'd done plumbing and everything else. One of those guys we're talking about, he said, One comes out of my house the other day, and he said, I saw him coming. I got outside before he could see that I came out of the house. I just walked out and I passed him. He says, No, you try and hear. He says, There's no chance. He says, The other guy turned around too and he walked back.

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: There used to be quite a few on the train, even though they didn't bother him too much for a while there. They'd be on there with their blankets going back and forth. Getting along now because those days each fella took his own chance, you might say, or more on your own. On the railroad was quite an interesting thing, that when the passenger train, they usually passed, it was two trains, two passenger trains each way. One of them, a day train, had a dining car on it and a night train had a sleeper on it. They'd pass the Juliaetta, or here, and if they passed it, Kendrick, we used to get a return trip ticket to Juliaetta and ride up on one and catch them back against us for the ride. But one of the great pastimes on Sundays was to go meet the trains. The platform would just be full of people on Sundays when the train come in. You'd see the train come in and see two of them there, then wait for the next train and people would visit, and that was our visiting place. And then of course those days, the mail would distribute it then, and you got your mail afterwards. We had mail service those days, but now we don't have any mail service anymore. You could get your mail every day of the week, holidays and all.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: Well, when were the Bums most, or the Hobos most around on the railroads?

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: Oh, I don't know. I just remember back there, and at one time it was a little tough in there, about 19.5 or 6 in there. I thought, I believe that quite a lot of them are riding back and forth. They'd take different trains. Now some of us fellas, we'd freight train go along and wasn't going too fast or something, and get someplace we'd get on it and go. And even the passenger train, another fellow and I one time got up here at Kendrick, passenger train standing there. And I went back, I'll catch you, and there's kind of a platform up there. I said to the fellow back yard going up there and riding her down to Juliaetta, that's where he's going. I didn't no more say it, and he's up there. I didn't back out, and I went up too, and we sat on that board at Juliaetta there. There was a big crowd there, watched the train come in, but the headlights blinded them all, they couldn't see us. They didn't anyway, and we got down there, we got off and walked uptown. Nobody ever knew we was on there, but it was kind of funny riding it seemed when you got to a curve that the blame thing wasn't going to go around the curve. The front end just kept on going out, out over the creek. But we rode it down to Juliaetta on the cow catcher.

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: I'll tell you, those days, things, you're more on your own, and I don't know, you can take care of yourself more. For instance, you take there when I was a youngster, you had a shotgun and a.22. If we wanted a few grouse or pheasants and go out and shoot a couple or three out there in the canyon, you didn't have any license or nothing. We'd shoot squirrels. If you wanted to go fishing and get your fishing pole, we'd go down and get us two fish. You didn't need a license to do anything. For instance, even in 1920, at day ..., I was starting to garage up here. We had a money drawer where the money was in. This money drawer that was in the office, and we got a dollar or two, we'd put it in there. When we had a little more money than we thought we were leaving the drawer, we'd divide it out. Each one would take half and put it in his pocket. When we'd go over and eat the restaurant, and neither one of us made, we'd just take a little money out of the drawer. We never kept track of anything. All the gasoline from Pullman would send a truck up there, take a truck and bring down about a bunch of 50-gallon barrels we had, sell our gas. The only thing we paid was taxes. End of the year, property taxes. Didn't worry about anything else. I look at it now. That was 1920 and 1921.

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: In those years, in 50 years, there was sure a bunch of had it on, wasn't there? Those days, you didn't need no hunting license. They did come in then, but that doesn't bother you. I never had any of those days. Never had any fishing license, hunting for fish and everything else, whatever they was. That's why you just did it, and that's the size of it. Anything you do, you kind of do it on your own. It's your own chances you're taking. What you're doing, like riding the trains or something like that, is just more or less up to what chances you took.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: What do you think started to change that?

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: Well, the progress, I guess you might say. I think that's about to take it. This kept you getting going a little more. You have to have this, and if you're going to have to have the paved highway, you're going to have to get some money someplace. We didn't have those. We had tuck holes there, and in the streets up here, at..., we put some signs out in the mud holes, no duck hunting allowed. It's for a joke. The automobiles, about October, people take them home and leave them home and put them up on blocks and take a battery out. He and I serviced the batteries, charged them, kept them charged through the wintertime. We'd have as high as 150 batteries in our shop there, just keep them charged. There was no cars running or anything else, but we'd overhaul some cars for people and rebuild batteries and work on cars like that. It would be used after Easter before there'd be much going, unless they did freeze sometime, and some would take the car out in winter. The slits broke a pretty good track, but of course they were narrower. Sometimes we'd go out, I know we used to go out to ride motorcycles. We used to go out in the winter and wrap a rope around for a chain and go in the snow.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: Grab a rope around the tire?

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: Yeah, wrap a rope around the tire and cut it with a chain. If I had my first motorcycle in 1911, I had an Indian motorcycle, I bought it second hand, single cylinder. It was direct connected, the pedals would go around. It had a brake in it, coaster brake, but in order to start it, you had to pedal it. So you'd either get on it and pedal it and kind of go downhill a little to start, or else run by the side of it. Then drop your valve, hold your valve open and twist your handle, which would release the valve. Then start, then jump on and go. The next one I got is a twin cylinder one. I went to Spokane and bought it in 1912, I think it was. It took me outside of town up there, and I came down on the dusty roads. There was a piece of... in there around Waverly, it came through that way. The dust kept a-polluting the road with this dust. I think it was getting late in the fall, and it just looked like it was raining right behind me. I made it home, got in the yard down at Juliaetta, and I started up towards the house, and a kiplunk and a sink quit right there. I shoved it away, started raining pretty soon. There wasn't a riding, but the crankshaft between the two flywheels broke on the motorcycle I had. I was that lucky to get home for all that it went through all the way there. I overhauled it then, and didn't get to ride it until I think it would've been winter sometime.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: Wouldn't there be a guarantee or something on it if you bought it new like that?

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: It was a second-handed one. The first one I think I paid $85 for it, and I sold it for that. The next one I paid $125, and I think I sold it either about $100, I believe it was then, that the brother got the automobile in 1915. He was working in the garage, and bought a between-ness and bought a match-all. The first ones were headlights and a battery starter.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: When you were a young man, what was the social life around Kendrick like? What kind of things did you do?

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: Well, after school, sometimes on the way home, some of the boys would stop, and we'd play catch or play ball, something like that. Generally, it was working, farming or hoeing or something. They'd be a show in town for ten cents. Occasionally, we'd go see that. Later on, there was some roller skating, and up here at Kendrick, we used to come up here to roller skate. At the end of most of it would be go squirrel hunting. I got on the outside, I'd go along the creek, go fishing, or just muck around along the creek someplace and wade around. Or play ball. In the wintertime, we'd be brought together, and maybe play card games or something like that. Of course, Sundays, they'd be neighbors get together, too. Coasting, if there was any snow on the ground. After we got motorcycles, some other boys got motorcycles. We used to go out Sunday mornings and go up on the hills or someplace to motorcycles, and probably go until something happened to them, and then fix them up again during the week and ride them again the holidays. But we used them on the telephone work by little there, then, until we got the car. Then we used this, we still had to use team until, oh, I don't think we'd discard the team until 1920 or so, before you could go. Then you'd have to hire livery rakes to take you out.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: Well, did there used to be Saturday Night Dances or anything here in Kendrick?

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: Yeah, they would use the dances. It seemed like country boys didn't get out very much to the dances. I didn't start to go dances until later on when they got in the garage business here, and one thing or another… they'd have dances.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: What kind of affairs were they? What kind of dances were they?

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: They had a dance in the Odd Fellows Hall up here and then in the Skating Rink down at the other places. They used to have an orchestra. They had a home orchestra that played, and they'd have old-time pieces. Missouri Waltz, three o'clock in the morning, and some of those pieces. They had just regular dances. It wasn't the kind that they'd step off now, you know. Yeah, and now it's time to change. If somebody get on the dance floor now dressed like the Arab boy, they'd have them in the...

speaker: Rob Moore
words: Talking about the guys who used to ride the rails, you know, were there ever any IWWs around here?

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: There used to be some go-through, and of course the whole goal, they got to call them all IWWs. I'll tell you, those fellas had a hard life, you know. They didn't have anything. There was no welfare or anything else. It is just what you'd give them. For some of the out-times, somebody hit me up someplace, and said, look, fella, I wouldn't give them any money, but I'd take them into the restaurant and tell them to give this fella, if they had, ask them what they had, if they had some stew or something, and they'd give them a bowl of stew, and here's the money for it, and feed them that much. Well, a lot of times they'd give them a little more, too, you know. I always figured, of course, some of them were different, but the hobo buns, they just, a bunch of people, they just didn't have anything. Times this hard. Now, people around home, it has just helped the neighbors. I can remember the neighbors there, we had a husband that grew up in the timber up here, with Bovill, and he'd just get back home once or twice all winter, and this woman had two boys and a girl, and they had a little garden there. Well, we'd give them apples and just lots of things like that, people just give them to them, and help them along, and one just helped the others, and the people you knew. I can remember people back, oh, since time, worked in telephones for a porter, that was back, say, 1910. It's 10 or 11. We'd go out in the country, and at the same time, we'd try to collect up some of the bills that people owed. And maybe a fellow owed his dollar a month, what was he, maybe owed six or eight, ten dollars. But sometimes, lucky, he says, well, we can spare you, we'll give you, we can spare you a couple dollars, and that'd be the size of it, but they seemed like they'd always make it, but then they had the income once a year, and they'd run out until the crops come in, and it is more of a whole lot more sociability about people, that if anyone was sick, why the neighbors would be there, and they'd bring in the eats, and they'd help, you know, they wasn't left like they are now. Now, if anyone's sick, they really can't find anyone because they're on welfare. And it's just hard proposition that there's people who had to go out, but then they're generally busy.

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: You're just about, you got to go to a rest home or someplace. It's all right for the ones that got it, or even if they don't have it. Now they get this welfare, and they're usually taken care of. But those days, there was no such thing. There was a poor farm up out of Moscow, so they could go up on a poor farm.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: Where was that? Where was that?

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: Well, it was up north of Moscow, I'd say north, up along old Lake Lake Railroad Airways, out of town. It used to be just a general name of the poor farm, and whoever could work would do some work, and there they didn't, and that's where they were just up against it. They'd take them up to the poor farm, and the county would keep them going. But I don't know whether anyone got any county money. I don't think they did. If they had to ask for something, they'd just have to go to the poor farm and work what they could. And the rest of it, if they couldn't work, well, then they were taken care of, but nothing to brag. Some person would run that poor farm, and the farm and all, I think, if I remember right. They didn't have no nice, clean bed and stuff like they've got now. They just had to take care of their own. They'd have some blankets and stuff, and I guess it's more up to them to keep them clean, and one thing or other, and sleep in the bunkhouses and things that people, these younger generations, they don't know what it used to be for those people. Even for the kids, you know, that have something. I know the first bicycle. I was quite old. The other bicycle I had, I learned to ride on. The handlebars were broken off. I closed, but there's two pegs of wood stuck in there, and that's what the guy did it with. Didn't have a coaster break. The pedals went around at the same time, and I later bought a bicycle, a couple of different ones. But there wasn't too many that even had the bicycles. If you had a horse, go get the horse or go a foot. Well, if you ought to go very far, you'd go in the pasture to get a horse. But if it wasn't too far, by the time you went and caught your horse, you'd just well walk the town in a way. But riding a horse then wasn't fun like they take it to be now. We had to ride horses too much. That wasn't a treat. I'd cultivate a horse all day with a gunny sack for a pad underneath and sweat all the way through on a hot day. Two bits.

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: But to those days, it didn't take very many two bits to cap it at total assets. It was expensive, but it didn't take very much. You just had twice as much as you had before. This person watched it out of whether the folks ever had, I've never had any money to mount anything home. I don't know just what they did. Well, they bought the first binder. I can remember the first binder. I got it downtown. I went down with them, rode down, and they let me ride on the Draper on the platform coming home. Because I wasn't able to walk that far. I think they paid $150 for it on time and paid it off. Then we run that binder and bound for other people at a dollar acre. It used to be my job if we run a lead horse or lead team as a driver lead team. On the home place, there was an elite team first before I was able to do much. Whoever shot, I'd be out there dragging the bundles up to them before I could lift them up around. The person was out there, and as soon as he was able to do something, you had a job.

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: Of course, they were about shocked to hay those days. Then they stacked it and then run the threshing machine in between two stacks and thrashed off of the stacks. They didn't haul it in like they did later on. Sometimes it would be late, you know, and they could thrash later on. The weather didn't hold it back so much and get it and stack it up. Later, we had hay. We had hay in a barn and stacked. You'd sell it for $5 or $6 a ton. People come after hay. I'd go put some hay and get you $5. That's about what they had. That's $5 to spend for some clothes. My mother raised chickens and she used to get about 10-12 dozen eggs a day. We'd take them to town for groceries and things like that. Apples and potatoes and stuff like that. We had our own, gathered them up and had them put away.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: Did you raise your own grain for the chicken feed or what?

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: Grapes.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: Did you raise your own grain for the chicken feed?

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: Yes. Yeah, raise your own and leave them grounded. In 1908, Otto and I, we was at a warehouse there where they had a gasoline engine. We tinkered with it and we got one. We got ours first. We got one in 1908. We had tinkered around with some machinery before. We hooked this up onto a cord sheller and we had a grinder too that we could grind corn and grain. We had it and we'd usually raise maybe six, eight, ten acres of corn. Sometimes we'd run a wagon through out there and just pull the corn ears out right out there and throw them in the wagon. The rest of the father let it go down and some would cut it down and stack it. Then husk it as it needed afterwards and then shell it. Had a grinder there. We'd shell it with this power of the seller. First we turned it by hand as a larger one and put one ear in at the time.

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: We'd shell and have corn in the grinder. Feed that and wheat. If we didn't thrash, we'd keep a patch of wheat and put it around and then thrash it with horses. Just drive horses around it until it thrashed out and then fanned it out with a breeze. But not for chicken feed. It seemed like there was always something to do, apples to gather and sauerkraut to make. The potatoes to drink and gather apples for the winter. You'll get the cows as you'd left them past you and had to bring them down through a couple of gates and get them in the barn. Get them to feed if they were fed milk them. Then first they had this skim milk can of pans. Her mother put the milk in the pans and skimmed the cream off. They got the cream separator. As we grew up, it didn't take long. It had something to do. We had a grape patch. We had about a per unit acre of grape vines. We had about three or four acres of orchards at first.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: Mostly apples or what? Mostly apples?

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: Mostly apples. Some prunes, some plums, a few peaches, pears, apricots, cherries. There's a good mixture of variety. Early apples and later apples. I think wine sap was our most of the later apples. Then we had a few good eating apples. We'd make two or three barrels of cider and two or three barrels of wine. Most of it, a lot of it made vinegar out of it. Our cider those days was kind of a... People come, the folks that have the cider. We'd have cider anytime we wanted it, but we didn't care for it anymore. You get something, you don't care for it. We had bees. We had our own honey. But we'd take it to town, trade it for syrup. We'd get tired of the honey, but syrup tastes better. Yes, I don't know. We had quite a bunch of bees one time. Sold honey. Anything to make a buck or two someplace. Then a cannery, later years, about 1913-14 in there. Cannery come into town. If there was anything like that, there's anything to learn to see in machinery. I remember this cannery when they set it up. They put the cappers in there. I spent quite a little time there. About the time I was getting ready to just to see how the thing worked more for curiosity. I kind of helped this fellow long, hand him stuff and see how I'd adjusted it. I remember working in the warehouse. When they put the cannery in, they wanted us to take some stock in this cannery. There's a stock company we didn't have any money to buy any stock with. We couldn't buy it in. They told us that people had stock. We were going to be the ones that would be having a job in this cannery. We had a job in the warehouse. They didn't figure, well, we just couldn't take it. We didn't. We had that cannery down there. They were working there at the warehouse. One of the fellas came over then. They said he noticed I was around quite a lot with that guy. If I wouldn't come over down and see if I could get straighten them out that the cans leaked. They couldn't keep them leaking. I went all down and I got it fixed so that I got adjusted so it wouldn't leak. I went back to the warehouse. I think I spent the rest of the day there keeping tab on it. They went to the warehouse. About a day or so they came over again. Now for me, 85 cents an hour if I would come down and just keep that capre going. That's all I had to do was watch that going. I get somebody else to take my place to finish out the warehouse. I went down. I kept the capre going. Whenever there was towards the end, I used to fire for them and whatever they were to cook them to and everything else. I worked there. That was good pay. I went 30 cents an hour to the warehouse. I got in off a good time. I would start seven in the morning. A woman would quit at six, I believe it was, five or six. We had all the canning to do yet what this can that they had put up and then clean up and one thing. He never gave it up, eight or nine. There was about 100 women worked there. There's a squall of tomatoes. Then they'd bring them in these baskets. Maybe about three or four screen diggers and dump them in their dish pans. They'd pair them and put them in cans and grade them. The first grade went in a pile. This kind of pile, the chain went on by. There where they could set them on and they'd go on. First they'd pile them up. Then after they'd get enough pile, then they'd start this chain and this heat. They would go through and slow progress through a heater cabinet. They must have been in there, but they'd be in there about two minutes and get steamed up good. They wouldn't bust when they cooked. They'd go through that and then they'd come to the machine. They'd go through the machine and they usually can. They had a big tray. They had 120 on one tier. They'd put in two tiers and hold 240 cans. They'd lick them and then they'd put them in and cook them in water and cool them. I remember at the most record time they put in a little over 10,000 cans in one day. It was a bunch of tomatoes. They'd get an ounce.

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: They also had a canner in Lewiston. They had trouble down there one time. I canned their Juliaetta. They started at five o'clock at seven in the morning. They wanted me to get down to Clarkston in the evening. We finished the Juliaetta. They took me down to Clarkston. They had it piled up there all day scanning. They got the machine adjusted and canned all night and cooked them too then. Down there, they'd come back again at seven o'clock in ... and went around. Then another time, Mahon charged over it and he asked, he says, fella, John Glenn up here, he's got 50 tons of prunes he'd like to sell. He says, if you want to, he says so we can can those after supper sometime. If you want to work evenings. I said, it's all right as far as I'm concerned. It didn't take only a few of us. We'd only put hot boiling hot water on them and get them hot and canned them in gallon cans. That was a different machine to can those with. We took on those 50 tons of prunes and canned them after supper. I figured I'd just hit the gold mine that time for the wages I got and the time I put in. That really kind of put me on my feet. I felt pretty independent after that. When I bought an automobile, I then spent it again. When this automobile had it and had about everything spent, then this telephone business came up. We bought it, but we had to borrow the money on that. Then we didn't know more than how one company bought that the other one was wanting to sell. We took them on too, but we bought them on a longer lease as interstate. We kind of doubled up pretty fast there, but how to work nowhere. I had my garage here then. I worked at warehouse and telephone and different places. Then I went over and worked in the Navy Yard over in the machine shop until the war was over. To come back, I helped different jobs. I helped the lumber office. Not that time. I helped at the garage and helped on the home place, put it in down there at Juliaetta. I'd go out and teach people how to drive automobiles. I'd sell automobiles here and I'd have to go up there for a day or two and stay with them and show them how to run the things. Just odd jobs. It sounds like you were the tide of progress around here. Yeah. Then I went. Debo and I bought out. That was Brother-in-law. He was married. He farmed up here on the ridge. We bought out the garage up here. We went in the garage business and rebuilt batteries. He'd done welding and overhauled cars for two years and a half. I sold out to his brother. I liked the outdoors better. I did work, at the meantime, in the garage, line work for the power company and one thing. I didn't like that better. I sold out to his brother. I went down to California and I worked down there for a telephone company then. Then I came back up here. Wilmont talked me in the ocean. It happened to me in a while. He did that. The first thing I knew, he said, you can have this job as long as you want to.

speaker: Herman Schupfer
words: It's kind of temporary, but I stayed with it. Then I sold to Washington Water Park. A temporary job lasted until I retired in 1967. Oh, 1957. I've been out for 15 years.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: Jumping back for a second. Did they ever find out how that cannery and Juliaetta burned?
